Have you ever zoned out on a Zoom call, then realised you’ve missed the last two minutes? I’ve been trying Wispr Flow’s Notetaker, which records and transcribes meetings in real time. You can ask it what you missed, search previous meetings for specific decisions, and use the transcripts with tools like ChatGPT and Claude to draft follow-up emails or messages. Very useful if, like me, you spend a lot of time in meetings, and even more time trying to remember what actually happened in them. A UTI can become much more than a urinary problem for older women. On unPAUSED, we discuss how these infections can become serious and potentially lead to sepsis. We also explore a possible connection between infection-related confusion, falls, and hip fractures. A woman who becomes confused, tries to get out of bed to use the bathroom, and falls may be facing more than one health crisis at once. It’s a conversation that shows why urinary health deserves more attention as women age. ✨Listen to the full conversation at the link in my bio.  #uti #womenshealth #menopause #hormonehealth #healthcare

Menopause weight gain isn’t a willpower problem. Your scale can barely move while your body changes underneath it: more fat around your organs, less muscle, and an appetite system working against you. A review published in September in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences pulls together 25 years of research on what falling estrogen does to appetite. Estrogen helps run the hunger switch in the hypothalamus; when it falls, the balance tips toward hunger. Leptin, the hormone that tells your brain you’ve had enough, rises, but the brain responds to it less. Ghrelin, your hunger hormone, dips after a meal but climbs back faster. The menopause guideline most OB-GYNs have practiced under was written in 2014, before the newest nonhormonal drugs existed and before the FDA changed the hormone therapy label. On October 15, ACOG replaced it: Clinical Practice Guideline No. 13, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology (2026), covering hot flushes, sleep, and mood. Hormone therapy is strongly recommended for hot flushes and the sleep disruption they cause, started before 60 or within 10 years of menopause; continuing past 60 may be necessary if symptoms persist.
